en: The Sūtra on the Absence of Expectation, translated by the Tripitaka Master Dharmarakṣa of the Western Jin Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Vulture Peak Mountain in the city of Rājagṛha, together with a great assembly of bhikṣus.
There were five hundred people in the assembly, and sixty thousand bodhisattvas.

All were great sages who had attained mastery of supernatural powers and achieved dhāraṇī; their eloquence was perfected and unimpeded, and they proclaimed the Way of the Sūtras with ever-consistent speech. Their supernormal transformations were inconceivable, and they were fully endowed with all practices, universally penetrating everything without exception.

Their names were: Bodhisattva Unimpaired Progress; Bodhisattva Resonance of the Thundering Voice of Deliverance; Bodhisattva Moon-Blossom of the Night; Bodhisattva Rain of Great Thunderous Speech; Bodhisattva Contemplating the Boundless Realm of Deliverance; Bodhisattva Arising from the Mountain Peak; Bodhisattva Joyfully Causing Delight; Bodhisattva Stainless and Unassailable Light; Bodhisattva Resolving the Nature and Meaning of Sentient Beings; Bodhisattva Attaining Strength as Firm as a Vajra; Bodhisattva Most Sublime Among All Sounds; Bodhisattva Transcending the Majestic Voice of Brahmā; Bodhisattva Renowned for Sovereignty, Terrifying and Unassailable; Bodhisattva Accumulating Roots of Virtue Like a Heap of Jewels; and Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta. With these as their leaders, there were sixty thousand bodhisattvas.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra was dwelling in solitude, reflecting with single-minded concentration in dhyāna. Rising from his seclusion, he went to where the Buddha was.
At that moment, the World-Honored One was sitting beneath a tree, having attained the samādhi of the Silent Echo.

At that time, Śāriputra was staying at a distance from the World-Honored One. Seeing from afar the Great Sage’s majestic demeanor and his serene, harmonious, and elegant deportment, he immediately sought out grass and spread it to form a seat on one side. He sat down cross-legged, straightening his body so it did not lean, and having settled himself comfortably, he thought to himself:
"This is truly unprecedented!
The majestic spiritual power, radiance, and demeanor of the Tathāgata, the Truly Realized One, are beyond measure; he is the foundation of the path to peace and security.

For this reason, all living beings attain tranquility. Regarding the unsurpassed right wisdom they have attained, they extol his meritorious achievements, for they have fully realized all dharmas and possess universal penetration.
At that time, the Great Sage, tranquil and composed, arose from samādhi and raised his voice.

When Śāriputra heard the Buddha, the World-Honored One, raise his voice, a virtuous mind arose within him; having attained his original aspiration, he advanced to the Buddha’s presence and stood with single-minded devotion. Bowing his head in refuge, his heart leaping with joy, he immediately uttered these verses in praise:
“If there are sentient beings Who harbor no expectations, And have never given rise to attachment,..."
Wandering through the world amidst all the sūtras, rejoicing alone in equanimity,
one is then able to always practice patience regarding this Dharma of the sūtras.
Seeing their flaws and shortcomings, these individuals’ faith and understanding are like illusions, occurring spontaneously;
they discern all phenomena as being clearly like empty space, and seeing no self,
they then attain great peace.
Not dwelling on sentient beings, as if there were no sentient beings at all;
never having attained any conceptual thought, and not perceiving a self—only then is there great peace.
From the very beginning, they have never been joined together;
they are not deluded by signs of existence, nor do they give rise to them, nor do they abide anywhere.
When one no longer perceives a life-span, only then is there peace and security.
Not relying on sentient beings, one is then free from strife within the dharma-realm;
casting aside all conceptions of "persons" and being without manifold thoughts, one attains peace and security.
The Benevolent One toward all beings harbors no stinginess or envy;
dwelling in the Dharma, he is free from calculation and sees no weakness—only then is there peace.
If one practices patience, peaceful and harmonious, surpassing the multitude,
they will never behold the greed for contention; neither failing in diligence nor falling into indolence,
and not even conceiving the thought of "patience"— only then is there true peace.
With single-minded meditative reflection, the mind has no thoughts; having eliminated all confusion and agitation, one clearly understands all phenomena.
Abiding in equanimous concentration, when one does not even conceptualize meditation, only then is there peace.
Furthermore, one does not follow the teachings of the ignorant;
without harboring a sense of clarity, yet without being mired in delusion, and free from the notion of wisdom—it is only then that one finds peace.
Whether dwelling in seclusion or likewise in a village, one should cultivate equanimity toward these two states;
neither thinking only of the evils of the village nor longing for seclusion— this is true peace.
Fully engaged in alms-gathering, he does not think, "I am seeking food for my own body," nor does he lament;
practicing begging for food, he has no notion of "alms-gathering"—
this is what constitutes peace.
Accepting and wearing this physical form, one does not lament, saying, "I am clad in coarse robes";
by not being arrogant toward others, one then finds peace.
In accordance with the teachings of all Buddhas, abiding securely by their instructions,
one wears the three grades of robes without ever being separated from them; yet one does not harbor self-conceited thoughts,
nor does one feel self-satisfied, thinking, "I have not violated the rites"— only then is there true peace.
The subtle and wondrous Dharma does not calculate "self," nor does it cling to "sentient beings.
It does not boast, saying, "I am preaching the Dharma. It does not rely on sounds or echoes;
only then is there peace.
Without the notion of solidity, not dwelling on worldly occupations, with no thoughts of purity or turbidity harbored in the mind,
and the body performing no conditioned actions— this is what constitutes peace.
If one arises [from practice], yet has no thought of arising; if one stands or dwells somewhere, yet does not dwell upon that place;
if one exerts oneself with diligence day and night, walking in meditation according to the proper measure, and remains free from speech—this is true peace.
Whether acting or not acting, one should always be free from deluded thoughts; regarding extraordinary notions,
whether they pertain to the Tathāgata or to external teachings, one should not regard them as distinct, nor harbor thoughts of superiority— this is what constitutes peace.
Equal as empty space, there is nothing to transcend; with no thoughts of self or sentient beings in mind, seeing no distinction—only then is there peace.
If one realizes that all things are like illusions and transformations, as if they were dreams seen at night;
if one attains eloquence and maintains a mind free from forgetfulness; and if one wanders through the world like the moon reflected in water, without coming or going—only then is there true peace.
Clearly seeing the true reality, one perceives that what is called "the body" possesses not a single solid essence;
thus being able to awaken to and comprehend the quiescent Dharma, one ceases to engage in false conceptualization,
and only then does one find peace.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One praised Śāriputra, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!
Your knowledge is profound and far-reaching; you practice the meaning of wisdom to its ultimate conclusion!"
To discourse on the Dharma and have its words accord with the subtle return of the Way—
how joyful this is! Now, Śāriputra,
let all those bhikṣus and bodhisattvas who dwell upon Vulture Peak and those scholars who frequent it here, so that they may all assemble to receive and accept the teachings of the Way.
Then, Śāriputra immediately addressed the Buddha:
“I am not capable of requesting that they be assembled. Why is this? ”
"O Great Beings, your majestic virtue surpasses that of the dragons, and your path-knowledge is inexhaustible; it is beyond my reach.
At that time, the World-Honored One emitted light from his body, illuminating the trichiliocosm.

At that moment, the assembly of bodhisattvas from the Buddha-fields, having been illumined by this radiance, all gathered on Vulture Peak in the space of a single thought-moment. They approached the Buddha’s presence, prostrated at his feet, circumambulated him three times, and then withdrew to stand in mid-air.
The bhikṣus dwelling in seclusion and the various bodhisattvas came to where the Buddha was, prostrated themselves upon the ground, and withdrew to sit to one side.
The countless multitudes of hundreds of thousands of people from the great city of Rājagṛha also went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, and withdrew to sit to one side.
At that time, the World-Honored One, seeing that countless multitudes had all gathered together, raised his venerable countenance to gaze upon the face of Mañjuśrī and immediately smiled.
Mañjuśrī then rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and with palms joined, asked the Buddha:
"For what reason did you smile just now? What is the significance of this manifestation?"
"The Tathāgata, the Truly Realized One, has never rejoiced in vain.
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:
"Now, on Vulture Peak Mountain, there are ten thousand bodhisattvas who are all expounding a sūtra; the name of this sūtra is 'The Elephant Simile'."
"This was also discussed in the distant past.
When the Venerable Ānanda heard what the Buddha had said, he immediately rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, knelt with palms joined, and prostrated himself in homage, saying: "Excellent!"
World-Honored One!

Out of compassion for sentient beings, so that they may attain eternal peace, you should proclaim this Elephant Simile Sūtra. This Dharma is difficult to encounter and rarely heard by the multitude; we pray that you will preach it at this time.
All the various schools have gathered like clouds to listen to this sutra; they shall certainly attain a profound penetration into its luminous, obscure, and wondrous mysteries. Why is this so?
The Tathāgata, the Most Honorable and Truly Realized One, is peerless and without equal; he has no rival in the three realms.
Just now, as the Honored One gazed upon Mañjuśrī’s face, he smiled immediately. This was not without cause; there must surely be a meaning behind it.
The Buddha said: "Excellent, excellent, Ānanda!"
You have observed these extraordinary roots of virtue; that which you can recognize is such that wisdom cannot be limited. Ānanda!
Listen attentively and reflect upon it well.
"I shall explain to you the reason for my smile just now.
Thereupon, Ānanda and the great assembly received the instruction and listened attentively.
The Buddha addressed Ānanda:
"If there are sentient beings who have faith and delight in this Dharma, their every movement and gesture will be like the gait of an elephant.
Those who believe in this Dharma will move like great elephants and likewise with the stride of a dragon."
Those who love and rejoice in this Dharma of true reality take the lion’s stride; their every movement and gesture is noble and without peer.
The Buddha told Ānanda:

“The essentials of this sutra delight all bodhisattvas. This teaching of the sutra accords with the assembly of bodhisattvas; you should inquire and receive it, for their fundamental merits from past lives will then manifest before your eyes.”

After my passing, this sutra shall be entrusted to the bodhisattvas, so that they may hold it in their hands, maintain a tranquil will and settled mind as they take refuge in emptiness, reciting it with their mouths and contemplating it with their minds.

This Bodhisattva-piṭaka does not resort to bodhisattvas of meager merit and obscured vision; it does not resort to the persons of bodhisattvas who harbor malice, flattery, and hypocrisy; nor does it resort to the hands of bodhisattvas who are full of longing and deluded conceptualization.
At that time, the World-Honored One manifested a portentous sign to move Mañjuśrī.
Mañjuśrī, perceiving it immediately, thought to himself:

"I wish to inquire of the Tathāgata, the Truly Realized One, regarding the profound and far-reaching Dharma, which is beyond the reach of all Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, and which serves as the exemplary sign for the tracks trodden by the assembly of Bodhisattvas."
Mañjuśrī stepped forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"So be it, World-Honored One!
I now wish to pose a question to the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha; if I am granted permission, I shall venture to speak."
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī,
“Ask whatever you wish.
All those gathered in this great assembly have come together here, and they shall all receive my grace.”
Mañjuśrī then addressed the Buddha, saying:

“What is it called that enables a bodhisattva to establish all dharmas of meritorious achievement, universally manifest all bodhisattva practices, transform and enlighten countless and incalculable classes of sentient beings, and manifest all buddha-lands like the moon reflected in water?”
The Buddha said: “Excellent, excellent, Mañjuśrī!”
What you have asked merely sets forth the essentials; the Tathāgata shall now provide a complete and detailed analysis, so as to establish the merit of your virtuous achievements.
Listen attentively, listen attentively!
"Reflect upon this well.
Mañjuśrī and the great assembly received the instruction and listened.
The Buddha addressed Mañjuśrī:

"If there are bodhisattvas who practice six dharmas, they will also be able to fulfill the teachings on the meaning of the Path and establish themselves in all meritorious virtues. What are these six?
If there is a bodhisattva who practices the perfection of giving, bestowing all that they possess without stinginess or attachment;
who fully accords with and carries out the precepts without regarding their own person; who establishes the prohibitions and refrains from all evils;
who does not perceive a self yet understands the ultimate meaning; and who accomplishes patience, gentleness, and serenity, harboring no resentment in their heart.
Having seen this, one is liberated and does not remain in stagnation; through diligent and energetic effort, the body has no place of action. The mind harbors nothing and discerns all things;
with a single mind and right resolve, one dwells in the gate of liberation.

Understanding what is appropriate, one attains meditative absorption (*samādhi*); the mind is eternally at peace, yet does not crave a fixed state of mind. One elucidates wisdom as the work of the Path, and while observing that one’s own body does not leave the five destinies, one causes all places of birth to receive deliverance.
"These are the six dharmas.
When a bodhisattva practices and fully masters these dharmas, they will be endowed with the merit of all virtues.
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:
"Furthermore, there are six dharmas by which one fulfills this matter and establishes all methods of meritorious achievement. What are the six?
First, a bodhisattva goes to the hells to protect and rescue those suffering from the torments of burning and roasting, causing them to be reborn in the heavens."

Regarding those in the animal realm who are agitated and unsettled, or who are frantic and confused, failing to understand principles of meaning, he grasps their nature and manifests to them the gentle and subtle Dharma;
regarding those of low status, commoners, or minor clans, he reveals to them the position of power and nobility of a Wheel-Turning Sage King;
in all cases, he universally manifests among the five destinies of birth to equally open the way for their deliverance.

In whatever place they are born, they excel far beyond the masses; they clearly understand how to enter all Buddha-lands according to the occasion, yet remain unmoved within the Dharma-body. Without coming or going, they manifest universally throughout all Buddha-lands;
they produce ten trillion voices to proclaim the teachings so that each may hear them, while their minds remain constantly settled—neither partial nor biased, their nature vast and expansive.
"These are the six dharmas by which a bodhisattva establishes all meritorious achievements.
Mañjuśrī again asked the Buddha:
"What is meant by a bodhisattva gathering and protecting those in the hells so that they are reborn in the heavens?"
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:

“When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, through the meditative absorption of the Great Lotus Samādhi, goes to protect and deliver those in the hells, he causes all of them there to attain the peace of rebirth in the celestial realms. Because sentient beings are afflicted by suffering and distress, he manifests the most excellent palace of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven; seeing the causes of these calamities, they become weary of them and attain liberation from all their afflictions.

He preaches the sūtras for the sake of those in hell, enabling countless hundreds of thousands of beings to cross over the pains of hell. This is how a Bodhisattva protects and delivers those in hell from the suffering of burning and roasting, remaining ever in accordance with the Dharma without transgression.”
Mañjuśrī again asked the Buddha:

"What is meant by a bodhisattva’s gathering, protecting, and rescuing those who are agitated and bewildered among animals from their calamities, so that they are born into the human realm, a place of peace and happiness?"
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:
“A bodhisattva mahāsattva possesses a samādhi called ‘Quiescence.

When entering into the correct reception of this samādhi, he is thereby able to protect those who dwell among animals, causing their minds not to be distracted and their dispositions to be harmonious and joyful. Thus, they attain peace and security and are reborn among humans. There, he protects them in three matters by preaching the Dharma, establishing countless classes of sentient beings in the Way. This is how a bodhisattva protects animals from the calamities of delusion and confusion, causing them to be born as humans.”
Mañjuśrī again asked the Buddha:
“What is meant by a bodhisattva being born into a lowly, commoner family of humble lineage, yet subsequently attaining the peaceful virtue of a wheel-turning sage king (cakravartin)?”
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:
"There is a samādhi called 'Entering the Samāpatti of the Tranquil and Pure Mind.

By means of this samādhi, one transcends all classes of decay and causes them all to become pure. Although born into a lowly family, one then attains the peaceful virtue of a wheel-turning sage king (cakravartin). This is what is meant by a bodhisattva being born among the lowly commoners of humble lineage, yet receiving the peaceful virtue of a wheel-turning sage king."
Mañjuśrī asked again: "What is it,
World-Honored One, that is called 'the Bodhisattva universally manifesting birth in the five realms of existence while remaining transcendent and distinct from sentient beings'?"
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:
"There is a samādhi called 'Illumination that Dispels All Conditioned Phenomena and is Extraordinarily Distinct.

When a bodhisattva enters this meditative absorption and dwells within it, they universally manifest throughout the five destinies to guide and lead sentient beings, enabling them to attain extraordinary and distinct practices, so that all may resolve to attain unsurpassed, true, and correct enlightenment."
Mañjuśrī again asked the Buddha:

"What is meant by a bodhisattva’s timely skillful means, whereby they universally enter all buddha-lands, yet remain unmoved from the station of their original dharma-body—neither coming nor going—and universally manifest all buddha-lands like the moon appearing in water?"
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī: "There is a samādhi called 'The Bodhisattva Entering All Sounds.

By means of this meditative absorption (*samāpatti*), one can, at that very moment, manifest one's own body throughout the ten directions—east, west, south, north, the four intermediate points, above, and below—without moving from one's place, neither coming nor going. Abiding in that meditative state, one beholds the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, of the ten directions and hears the sutras they preach. This is the bodhisattva’s skillful means of being immovable while manifesting everywhere in all buddha-lands according to the occasion; just as the moon appears in water without coming or going, so too the bodhisattva’s cycles of transformation involve no coming or going."
Mañjuśrī again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"What is meant by a bodhisattva manifesting ten trillion voices to proclaim the teachings so that each may hear them?
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:

Thereupon, the Bodhisattva attained the immeasurable *parivarta-dhāraṇī* (the dhāraṇī of infinite revolutions), thoroughly understanding the mental dispositions of infinite sentient beings; according to their respective languages, he articulated various sounds and voices, discerning countless resonant teachings and expressions to accord with their intentions and lead them toward their respective goals.

Upon attaining this dhāraṇī, one manifests all sounds so that they may be heard everywhere; each is expounded with words free from error. This is how a bodhisattva manifests ten trillion sounds, articulating teachings so that each being finds their proper place.
Thereupon, Mañjuśrī came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Indeed, World-Honored One!
The skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*) of the bodhisattvas are difficult to fathom, exceedingly difficult to fathom; they are transcendent and without peer.”
"This essential sūtra is that which all bodhisattvas constantly receive through study.
By what practice does one attain the gate of faith and liberation?
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:
"A bodhisattva who wishes to study this sutra should have faith and understanding in the gateway of emptiness.
He then asked the World-Honored One:
"What is meant by emptiness?"
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:
“That which is called space is void and non-existent; it is free from defilement and possesses no mind of malice or harm, nor does it ever forget.”
All phenomena are likewise thus: they are undefiled and unharmed, and there is no forgetting them.
They are like space; they do not constitute giving, nor do they possess morality, patience, diligence, concentration, or wisdom, for they are eternally beyond reach.
Thus it is, Mañjuśrī!
All dharmas do not constitute giving, morality, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, or wisdom.
Just as space, for this reason they are neither to be liberated nor eliminated; all dharmas are likewise neither to be liberated nor eliminated.
Just as in space, there is no agent who acts and nothing that is realized, so too it is with all phenomena: there is neither activity nor realization.
Just as space is neither dark nor luminous, so too are all phenomena: they are neither dark nor luminous.
Just as space is vast, boundless, and cannot be grasped, so too are all phenomena: they are universally without limit and cannot be grasped.
Just as space has neither a correct path nor a deviant track, so it is with all phenomena: they have no path and no track, nor do they possess deviation or correctness.

It is just like space: it does not establish a body and is free from all outflows of conditioned activity; it does not train as a śrāvaka, does not aspire to the level of a pratyekabuddha, and does not cling to the unsurpassed Mahāyāna of the Buddhas. All dharmas are thus: they do not train as śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, or followers of the Mahāyāna.
Just as space is without thought and without discrimination, so too are all phenomena: they are without deluded imagination and without discrimination, just like space.
There is no uplifting, no lowering, no advancing, and no slackening; all phenomena are thus, being neither advancing nor slackening.

Just as space has nothing that corresponds or does not correspond, nothing dual or singular, so too are all phenomena: they have nothing that corresponds or does not correspond, and likewise neither duality nor singularity.

Just as space universally illuminates all sentient beings without being able to be defiled or rendered impure by dust, so too are all dharmas; even unto parinirvāṇa, they are forever free from defilement.

For this reason, it cannot be extinguished nor can it be removed; it is like space, which has nothing established within it and no place where it dwells, for it is unmoving, unshakable, and without location.
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:

“A bodhisattva mahāsattva understands that all sentient beings have no place of abiding; they should not observe them as having a location. They reach the ultimate limit (pūrvakoṭi), which is unmoving, unshaking, non-abiding, and yet not non-abiding.”
The Buddha said: "It is so, Mañjuśrī! That Dharma is spontaneous;
for one who wishes to see the Tathāgata, the Arhat, as a substantial entity, that constitutes a false view."
Those with wrong views seek to enter right view;
that which is right view is nirvāṇa, not a fruit of great virtue nor a matter of great merit.
Once one has reached nirvāṇa—being neither a fruit of great virtue nor possessing merit—one is a benefactor to the world.
That World-Honored One has no expectations regarding the World-Honored Ones;
having no expectations regarding the World-Honored Ones, he is then able to fulfill the wisdom of empty stillness;
having fulfilled the wisdom of stillness, he is then able to swiftly achieve the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
At that time, sixty bhikṣus in the assembly were all filled with great arrogance, each thinking to themselves:
"Now the Tathāgata proclaims these teachings on the dark paths and delusions; such words exist among all the heterodox and false schools—what use are they for practice?"
Just as the World-Honored One previously expounded this teaching regarding Pūraṇa Kāśyapa, Mahā-Moggallāna, and Ajita Keśakambalin,
so now do Sañjayin Vairaṭīputra, Kakuda Kātyāyana, and Nirgrantha Jñātiputra all speak these same words.
For what reason does the Tathāgata also expound these words? What is their distinction?
How should one follow them?
What should be practiced, and what should be taken as one's task?
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing the thoughts in the minds of those sixty bhikṣus who harbored great pride, immediately addressed Mañjuśrī:

“The Buddha, as a Tathāgata, Arhat, and Samyaksaṃbuddha, proclaims the sūtras; yet he does so in a manner identical and without distinction from the heterodox teachers and other scholars. Furthermore, these heterodox teachers are unable to discern the ultimate destination of the meaning of the Dharma taught by the Tathāgata.”

As soon as those sixty bhikṣus heard these words, their sorrow and distress increased and their minds were not gladdened; they had no desire at all to respectfully delight in the exposition of the meaning of this sutra, so they rose from their seats and departed immediately.
Mañjuśrī addressed the bhikṣus: "Virtuous ones!
Where do you wish to go?"
Then the bhikṣus replied to Mañjuśrī, “We do not understand this Dharma that has been taught; to what does it lead?
At that time, Śāriputra addressed the bhikṣus:
"Venerable friends! This meaning is excellent;
we should once again clarify its intent by means of this matter."
"Wait but a moment; I shall inquire of the Tathāgata, the Truly Realized One, as to why he has spoken this.
When the bhikṣus heard Śāriputra proclaim these instructions, they returned to their original seats.
Then Śāriputra stepped forward and asked the Buddha:
"For what reason has the Tathāgata proclaimed these words, causing all the bhikṣus to harbor doubts?
We only pray that the World-Honored One will, out of compassion, bestow his grace and resolve this web of confusion."
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Śāriputra:
"What do you think?
If there were a bhikṣu whose outflows were exhausted, whose mind was liberated, and who was free from all remaining fetters, would he harbor doubt or feel fear upon hearing this teaching?"
He replied, “No, World-Honored One.”

One who has already seen the truths practices the conduct of a bhikṣu; regarding all sounds and all spoken words, they feel no fear, no terror, nor any apprehension—how much less so for a bhikṣu whose outflows are exhausted, whose mind is liberated, and who is free from all remaining fetters and doubts?
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
“There may be some foolish people whose minds are obstructed and shrouded in darkness; regarding these unprecedented dharmas, they harbor deluded thoughts and pursue empty, vain practices.”
Then Śāriputra again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I pray only that the Great Sage would explain the intent of these scriptural passages, so that all those gathered here may cast off their lingering doubts and their minds may become serene."
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"If there were someone who saw the Tathāgata in a dream, would they truly see the form of a real person?

The Tathāgata says that what is beheld in a dream is not real; it is neither firm nor essential, for it arises entirely from mental ideation, the conceptualization of what is ideated, and the thorough absence of any fixed thought."

When there is no perception of conjunction and nothing exists, one then understands that the Tathāgata has no perception of discrimination, no perception of investigation, and no perception of harboring thoughts.

When there is no perception of conjunction and nothing exists, one then understands that all sentient beings and all phenomena are entirely illusory and lack reality; thus, one is able to clearly comprehend how all dharmas are characterized by delusion, inversion, and negligence.
Having already been able to thoroughly understand the delusions regarding all phenomena, the Tathāgata fully proclaims these delusions and false views.
Having already been able to discern that all phenomena are entirely false views, he no longer follows after delusion, false doubt, or the sixty-two views.
This is it, Śāriputra! If anyone wishes to contemplate the Tathāgata as being truly existent, they fall into false views. Therefore, Śāriputra!
The Tathāgata has said this:
if anyone wishes to contemplate the body of the Tathāgata, they fall into false views;
only by eliminating the conceptualization of seeing and hearing can one contemplate the Tathāgata, and thus be free from false views.
Then Śāriputra again asked the Buddha,
saying: "What, World-Honored One,
is meant by causing those with wrong views to enter into right view?"
The Buddha told Śāriputra:

"All foolish and ignorant ordinary people, regarding all their deluded thoughts—whether they correspond to what is appropriate or inappropriate—give rise to them and establish them within various bases. They do not believe in these matters; they have no foundation for either diligence or indolence, being neither dual nor singular. They give rise to views of a self-body, a person, and a life-span, relying upon and calculating 'I' while greedily clinging to a self, yet they claim to understand and discern."

Such forms and appearances as are seen, heard, recollected, or known, and the joy and pleasure derived from what is spoken—all these are non-existent. Thus, that which exists is scrutinized and found to be non-existent; this is what is called "that which is produced" and "that which is unproduced," "the false" and "the real"—all such words are non-existent.
That which is false and illusory should be understood as being without peer and without image; yet, because it is without peer, it constitutes a wrong view.
The Buddha said to Śāriputra:
"To see such illusions in this manner and to understand them without being deluded—this is called a wrong view, and it is identical to the wrong views of the non-Buddhists."
For this reason, Śāriputra,
one should know that by falling into wrong views, one conditions the attainment of right view.
Śāriputra again asked the Buddha:
"What is meant by giving with right view such that the merit is not great and the karmic reward does not extend far?
The Buddha told Śāriputra:

"If there were someone who gave such a gift as this, giving it to those who are the Benefactors of the Multitude, they would thereby accomplish the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) and draw near to the unconditioned.
As for that which is unconditioned, it possesses no small merit nor great achievement; it has no minor renown, nor even great renown."
"Why is this? Because that which is unconditioned is entirely free from the retribution of all meritorious achievements and has no location.
At that time, Śāriputra again asked the Buddha:
"How does the Tathāgata, the Arhat, speak of the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) as being without location?
Originally he praised the unconditioned as the most extraordinary, its merit and power being limitless."
The Buddha told Śāriputra:

"Foolish ordinary people possess abundant conditioned activities and calculate the existence of a self, others, a life span, and a soul. For this reason, the Tathāgata extols the immeasurable merit of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) to reveal its locus;
wishing to cause all beings to sever the afflictions of birth and death, he praises that which is extraordinary."

Furthermore, Śāriputra! You should examine the noble ones (ārya): they are neither merely noble nor merely holy, yet they are not those who lack the blessings of the multitude. You should cultivate this contemplation to achieve the state of a noble one.

Those who have abandoned desire and possess the blessings of the multitude are like farmers: according to what they sow, each reaps its corresponding kind; yet, relying upon the grain seedlings, there may arise the defects of thorns, weeds, and impurities.
Śāriputra, what do you think?
Is this report from the farmer true?
Did he originally plant thorns, weeds, and impurities?
Śāriputra replied, “No, World-Honored One.”
The Buddha said, "It is so, Śāriputra."
Suppose, Śāriputra, as when a farmer sows seeds in the earth, and instead of [the desired crop], thorns arise depending upon it, and the fertile ground is transformed into weeds.
It is even so, Śāriputra!
If one gives to the worthy and noble with the desire to establish merit but cannot find joy in it, this is not a good seed; it will not bear fruit, and one will likely gain nothing at all.
If one does not establish the field of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), then one should know that the retribution of birth and death (*saṃsāra*) will follow.
"Therefore, Śāriputra, those who wish to attain equanimity—
this equanimity of the unconditioned— is neither great merit nor a great achievement.
Then Śāriputra again asked the Buddha:
“Yes, indeed, World-Honored One!
What cultivation of the unconditioned results in neither great merit nor great achievement?”
"Regarding the merit of bestowing gifts upon such as these, how does one become a benefactor to the world while remaining in it?
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"If one does not harbor the notion of small merit, nor the notion of great merit, this constitutes planting the virtue of being a benefactor to the world."

Having already been able to plant the merit of the manifold blessings, his brilliance shines everywhere without exception, and he does not receive karmic retribution; this is the supreme benefactor among all classes of beings in the world.
If, Śāriputra, one establishes such a gift, it is an inexhaustible field of merit; yet they do not receive its flowers nor obtain its fruit.
For this reason, such a giver possesses neither great fortune nor great merit; though they are a benefactor to the world, they do not receive a karmic retribution.
Śāriputra again asked the Buddha: "How is this so,
World-Honored One?"
"If one acts for the sake of bestowing blessings upon the multitude and enters into the multitude of blessings,
will there not be the reception of karmic retribution? The Buddha said, "Śāriputra, what is your intention regarding this?"
"The merit bestowed by such giving relies upon the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); furthermore, do you reckon that this dharma has a retribution?
Śāriputra replied to the Buddha, "No."
World-Honored One!

When one bestows the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) as a gift upon the field of merit, there is no retribution received and thus no fruit of realization; that which is unconditioned has nothing to be sought, and even the noble sages have nothing to expect from it.
Then the Buddha praised him, saying:
"Excellent, excellent, Śāriputra!"
"It is exactly as you have said: he is the Benefactor of the World while dwelling among beings.
If anyone were to bestow this benefaction, they would have no expectation [of reward].
At that time, Śāriputra again asked the Buddha:
"How is it, World-Honored One?
How can there be giving without retribution, while being fully endowed with the wisdom of emptiness?"
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"If one is able to understand that all dharmas are entirely spontaneous,
is that meaning real, or is it false?"
He addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"One who can thoroughly understand that all phenomena are spontaneous (svabhāva) is able to discern that spontaneity as being like an illusion;
one who can thoroughly understand that all phenomena are like an illusion should realize emptiness through the wisdom of emptiness."
Why is this so? Because all phenomena are naturally like illusions; that which the Buddha described as being "like an illusion" refers to emptiness, the wisdom of emptiness.
Therefore, World-Honored One,
one thoroughly understands that all phenomena are naturally like illusions. Why is this so?
"Upon examining those dharmas, there is nothing accomplished and nothing obtained.
The Buddha said, "Excellent, excellent!"
Śāriputra! It is as you have said.

If there were any dharma that truly possessed a location, or if there were anything that could be grasped through the practice of contemplating ultimate truth, then one would no longer understand the meaning of the unconditioned parinirvāṇa of sentient beings; for all dharmas are empty and non-existent, lacking both ultimate truth and reality.

For this reason, although he transforms, delivers, and brings to nirvana sentient beings of the five destinies who are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, there is no decrease in the multitude of sentient beings; for all of them arise from the cause of emptiness and non-arising.
Thus it is, Śāriputra! Why is this?
Because that which sentient beings conceive is empty and non-existent;
what they think upon cannot be attained. For this reason, it is called "possessing the wisdom of emptiness."
"Therefore, that which is learned is employed to bestow blessings upon all beings; there is no fruit of retribution, for it is endowed with the wisdom of emptiness.
At that time, Śāriputra again asked the Buddha:
"In what way is the wisdom of emptiness fully perfected?"
"For this reason, one is able to swiftly attain the patience regarding the non-arising of all phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
The Buddha said,
"To not seek realization within emptiness and non-existence is what is called being endowed with the wisdom of emptiness and non-existence."
Furthermore, Śāriputra,
what is meant by "emptiness"?
It is knowing that the body is empty and non-existent, and that the self, persons, and life-span are likewise empty and non-existent.
One perceives that which is subject to cessation and yet calculates it to be permanent; though all phenomena are interconnected, they are likewise empty and non-existent.

This is because the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha are conceptions of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), which heal the mind’s various thoughts and ideations; for whatever the mind wanders through is entirely empty and non-existent.
Śāriputra! Those who are able to inquire about and receive such teachings as these shall realize this wisdom and thereby attain liberation. This, Śāriputra!
"Those who possess the wisdom of emptiness and discern things in this manner will be able to swiftly attain the patience regarding the non-arising of all phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
When these words were spoken, forty thousand bodhisattvas immediately attained the patience regarding the non-arising of all phenomena.

At that time, six thousand people resolved their minds upon the Great Way, and thirty-six thousand devaputras, having encountered this opportune moment of wisdom, were destined to draw near to the traces of the Path.

As for those sixty bhikṣus who harbored extreme pride, their outflows were exhausted and their minds were liberated, reaching the state of non-arising; with one voice and in unison, they raised their voices and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One! We—”

From this day forward, I shall follow the teachings of the Six Teachers and thereby leave the household life; the Buddha is not my teacher, I shall not receive his Dharma, and I shall not take refuge in the Noble Sangha.
From this day forward, I shall do nothing at all, nor shall there be any karmic retribution; I shall not commit grave offenses, nor shall there be any miserable realms of existence.
When the entire assembly heard this teaching, countless people were all struck with amazement and did not know what to think.
Each thought to themselves:

"These bhikṣus must be seeking to lead us astray; they have distanced themselves from the Buddha and contravened the Dharma, abandoning the prohibitive precepts to follow external heterodox teachings. This is why they now utter such words."
At that time, Śāriputra, knowing the thoughts in the minds of the assembled multitude, immediately addressed these bhikṣus, saying:
"Venerable sirs, why have you uttered these words:
'From this day forward, we shall have no Buddha, World-Honored One; therefore, we shall leave the heterodox teachers and become śramaṇas'?"
At that time, the bhikṣus replied to Śāriputra:

“From this day forward, we shall respectfully serve the six teachers; all that we take refuge in is but a single characteristic. We do not rely on the six sense bases, and for this reason, we do not perceive various kinds of Buddhas, nor do we conceive the thought of leaving home to become śramaṇas.”
Śāriputra asked again:
"For what reason, O worthy ones, do you speak these words once more:
'From this day forward, we shall no longer regard the Buddha as our holy teacher'?"
The bhikṣus replied: "From this day forward, we shall dwell in our own land and not in foreign lands;

we shall take refuge in ourselves and not in others; we shall make ourselves our own masters and not employ another as teacher. For this reason, we shall go [to other places] without regarding the Buddha as our holy teacher."
"Why is this? Because that Buddha, the Perfectly Awakened One, is not separate from the self, and that self is not separate from the Buddha.
At that time, Śāriputra again questioned the bhikṣus:
"O worthy ones! Why do you say again:
'From this day forward, we shall no longer receive the Dharma, nor take refuge in the Noble Sangha'?"
The bhikṣus replied: “We do not find any dharmas toward which we can turn our thoughts for refuge, nor is there any assembly [of them]; therefore, we do not take refuge in the Dharma or the Saṃgha.
Śāriputra again asked the bhikṣus:
"Why did you speak thus:
'From this day forward, there shall be no karma created, nor anything to be done'? The bhikṣus said:
"From this day forward, I clearly understand that all phenomena are entirely without action; yet that which is without action is not non-action either.
For this reason, from now on, I shall perform no further deeds."
At that moment, Śāriputra asked again:
"Virtuous ones!
For what reason did you just now say:..."
"From this day forward, there shall be no karmic retribution.
The bhikṣus replied, "Out of foolish companionship and lack of understanding,
we have pursued the cycle of birth and death, remaining entangled from beginning to end."
"We are utterly foolish, devoid of conditions and devoid of retribution; for this reason, from this day forward, there shall be no karmic fruit.
Then Śāriputra asked them again, "O virtuous ones!..."
"For what reason did you further utter these words:
'From this day forward, there shall be no further calamity or transgression'? The bhikṣus said:

"We have realized that all dharmas are quiescent and transcendent; we have understood that all dharmas are without self-nature and without retribution. Because all dharmas possess no karmic fruit, for this reason we utter these words:
'From this day forward, there shall be no further calamity or transgression.'"
At that time, Śāriputra asked again, saying:
"Virtuous ones, for what reason do you speak these words:
'From this day forward, there shall be no evil realms of existence'?"

The bhikṣus said: “From this day forward, we have clearly understood the destination of all dharmas; there will forever be no evil destinies for us. There is neither conversion nor non-conversion, neither discipline nor non-discipline.”
"For this reason, from this day forward, there shall be no evil destinies, nor shall there be any who do not proceed [to liberation], nor any who are neither disciplined nor undisciplined.

At that time, as the bhikṣus spoke such discourses on the meaning of abandoning self-conceit, three thousand six hundred bhikṣus among those who heard it attained the exhaustion of outflows and the liberation of mind, reaching the state of non-arising.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One praised the bhikṣus, saying:
"Excellent, excellent! To have nothing to obtain regarding all dharmas is itself true attainment."
He asked again:
“World-Honored One,
what is meant by ‘attaining something regarding the Dharma’?”
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī,
“What is called ‘attainment’ refers to reaching the patience regarding the non-arising of all phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Mañjuśrī asked again:
“If there is a bodhisattva who wishes to joyfully attain the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti), how should they train?
How should they establish themselves?
What is meant by practicing and following it?”
The Buddha then wished to explain:

"Mañjuśrī! Those who study the Unsurpassed Dharma and roam within the wisdom of all-knowledge and the meaning of the various supernormal powers should always practice and cultivate the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena."
At that time, the Buddha spoke in verse:
"If one aspires to learn the Buddha’s wisdom, The most honored among all who learn,
One does not grasp at any dharmas, Nor does one abandon anything at all."
The Dharma is without attainment, nor does it transcend accomplishment.
All phenomena are non-existent, yet the foolish desire to make them exist;
wishing to eliminate such conduct, he therefore preaches the Dharma for the multitude.
Turning back from the inclinations that give rise to worldly pleasure, one has no further cause for lack of faith;
if one can cast off the works of Māra, the Buddha-way is honored as unsurpassed.
If one gives birth to ignorance and delusion, one will therefore not understand this meaning.
Based on what has arisen in various ways, the ignorant perceive each differently.
Yet that which arises is not manifold; it is of a single characteristic.
The Buddha, the world’s luminous wisdom, explains this for the sake of ordinary people.
Because of clinging to the notion of "self," one is unable to practice the Way;
one should reflect that it will take a long time to utterly extinguish greed and lust,
distance oneself from hatred and the darkness of ignorance, and contemplate that one is free from worldly afflictions.
Perceiving existence where there is no existence, one cuts off and extinguishes even Nirvana.
To transform and civilize those with greed and anger, he speaks of tranquil emptiness;
because all is darkly exhausted and nothing is born, he extols Nirvāṇa.
To use expedient means to praise cessation [alone] is to remain far removed from the Buddha-dharma;
to harbor thoughts while practicing charity and observing precepts, or to hope for and delight in the Path,
is not to cultivate the Buddha’s teaching, but merely to pursue the study of conceptual thought.
The fool may be deluded, not understanding the dharma of emptiness;
they conceive of all phenomena as being uniform, yet harbor manifold thoughts.
If one clearly understands this dharma, one perceives all phenomena as being naturally so.
Just as one who contemplates their five fingers finds the Way is not difficult to attain;
the Way is neither far from people nor yet is it near.
By diligently seeking after delusive appearances, one therefore remains far from the Way.
The conduct of fools differs from one another; they constantly seek out each other's faults.
One person observes the prohibitions and precepts, while this other commits wicked transgressions.
Though they practice the True Dharma with virtuous deeds, all conditioned things are entirely empty and non-existent.
No longer receiving a conscious spirit, like an illusion there is nothing to be seen;
there is no mark of observing precepts, nor is there any committing of evil.
All phenomena arise from the conjunction of causes and conditions, and therein is no self.
Even if for billions of kalpas one practices peerless giving and maintains the supreme precepts,
the Guide will not grant a prediction [of enlightenment].
But if one has eliminated all conceptual thoughts and gives without any expectation of reward, [then he shall receive it].
Abandon all longing, and only then will you receive the separate instruction.
It is said that through giving one gains merit, and by observing the precepts one is born in heaven;
yet that which cannot be attained therein is the unsurpassed Way.
The fool relies on perversions and, through deluded thoughts, seeks after something;
I shall instead attain the patience of dharmas (dharmakṣānti), wherein there is no arising and no conditioned activity.
Regarding dharmas that have no source of birth, the mind does not conceive of anything being produced.
Upon attaining the patience regarding dharmas, one does not undergo further eons of billions;
though one provisionally proclaims the names of existing dharmas, all dharmas are without action,
without origin, and without abode— conceptions are all like empty space.
Countless billions of Buddhas proclaim the supreme and wondrous Dharma, causing the removal of lust, anger, and delusion; yet all phenomena are likewise inexhaustible.
Even if all phenomena were real, they would ultimately return to extinction.
Because they are non-existent, they cannot be apprehended.
Lust, anger, and delusion are immeasurable; when calculated, they have no limit or bottom.
Since they have no limit or bottom, they possess no fundamental root.
If there is no seed planted, how can flowers and fruit arise?
If even leaves are not obtained, by what cause could there be blossoms?
Since there are no dharmas from which they arise, there is likewise no person who plants them.
Sentient beings are not sentient beings; they neither arise nor cease.
They are like a wanton woman who has no son; because she has no son, she has no sorrow for a son.
The wise one contemplates thus: that all phenomena are unarisen;
he is then free from fear as he wanders through the suffering of birth and death.
The fool is deluded by falsehoods and does not understand that phenomena are like illusions.
One who takes up the burden of space will grow weary of the sublime and virtuous teaching.
If one were to analyze this teaching, it would be immeasurable, boundless, countless, and limitless; only then would one no longer grow weary.
As the Buddha taught regarding the limit of the past, he proclaimed it to be boundless and bottomless;
the limit of the future is likewise so, and the middle limit is of a single characteristic.
To conceive of a limit where there is no limit is a delusion; the bottomless limit is empty and void.
I have already realized this meaning, and thus liberation is non-dual.
The fundamental limit has the characteristic of space; the limit of persons is inconceivable.
That limit is like a shadow; this wisdom cannot be fully grasped.
Because one acts out of deluded thoughts, the mind thus regresses.
One must exhaust this net of [defilements]; by what cause could one attain Buddhahood?
In true awakening there is no conceptualization; therein, nothing is attained.
All phenomena are without arising, yet the ignorant desire to bring them into being.
Space cannot be grasped, nor can its various locations;
space has no place of abiding, for it is unconditioned and formless.
Just as one might praise empty space, so too should one understand the Way;
just as one distinguishes and realizes the Way, so too should one awaken sentient beings.
The realm of sentient beings is entirely equal, for it is equal to the realm of empty space.
One who can thoroughly understand these things will find it no difficult matter to attain the Buddha-way.
If one does not seek deliverance through diligence, does not contemplate with compliance,
and does not aspire for the various dharmas, there will be no difficulty in attaining the Buddha-way.
The Way is detached from all aspirations; it severs all essential vows.
When the mind harbors no seeking or longing, the Way of the Buddhas is supreme.
With a mind of giving, one reflects within oneself that through such practice, the Way is attained.
The Way is that which can be attained; the Supreme Way is that which yields no gain.
Their will is constantly fixed on prohibitions and precepts, and they imagine their diligence to be substantial.
Such persons do not follow the Buddha’s teaching, for they desire to seek a reward.
All dharmas are without diligent cultivation, yet they manifest as diligence;
that which has no practice—this is the supreme perfection of diligence.
When one gives rise to such a conception, these dharmas are free from all outflows.
This dharma is with outflows; that mind does not accord with it.
The dharma of non-thought which is taught is praised as being like space—neither bound nor liberated; this wisdom is unsurpassed.
Those who hope to uphold the precepts and those who imagine themselves violating the prohibitions—both of these violate the prohibitions; non-duality is the supreme prohibition.
All phenomena are without difference; they are without conceptualization and without distinction.
If one understands and penetrates the absence of views, this is truly to uphold the Buddha’s teaching.
When the mind gives rise to nothing, it is likened to empty space;
receiving such a definitive resolution with equanimity, one is then a practitioner of true tranquility.
For one who has no perceptions, who is entirely free from thoughts,
whose mind is without arising— such a person finds the Buddha-way not difficult to attain.
One who does not accept craving and is not driven by desire, [attains it as well].
If one is free from greed, there is nothing that arises; the Buddha-way is not difficult to attain.
If one does not weary of the succession of kalpas, does not fear the billions of fundamental limits, and does not dread the hardships of birth and death, the Buddha-way is not difficult to attain.
Thereupon, when the World-Honored One had finished reciting these verses, he addressed Mañjuśrī:

"If there are bodhisattvas or ordinary persons who have deep faith in this sutra, and upon hearing it do not doubt or harbor hesitation, but instead receive, uphold, recite, and explain it to others, fully understanding its meaning, they shall immediately attain the merit and virtue of twenty matters."
What are the twenty matters?
First, all the celestial deities and spirits will dwell by one's side;
second, the great kumbhāṇḍas and nāgas will come to protect one.
Third, all the great spirits and deities shall collectively protect them;
fourth, their minds will always be peaceful and secure, never experiencing agitation;
fifth, wherever they are born, they will become honored elders among the multitude.
Sixth, in every lifetime and wherever they dwell, they shall always possess the knowledge of past lives;
seventh, in each birth and in every place they reside, they shall always attain the five supernormal powers;
eighth, they shall swiftly attain the patience of the Dharma (dharmakṣānti) and, furthermore, shall behold Maitreya Bodhisattva.
Ninth: To single-mindedly and diligently cultivate the essentials of this sutra, casting from the mind all thoughts of sleepiness and exhaustion;
tenth: If, during times of sleep, one constantly beholds various Buddhas in dreams, one shall likewise behold various Bodhisattvas;
eleventh: By virtue of having profound faith in this sutra, one shall swiftly attain the patient acceptance of the compliant Dharma (*anulomikī-dharmakṣānti*).
Twelfth: If there are those who receive this sūtra, they shall, in the present life, attain the eradication of disputes and litigation.
Thirteenth: If one encounters serpents, vipers, or venomous insects, by recollecting this sūtra, one will ultimately have no fear.
Fourteenth: By contemplating this scripture, one will be able to subdue enemies, foes, and animosities.
Fifteenth: If one can single-mindedly contemplate this sutra, one will immediately attain the Samādhi of Universal Radiance;
sixteenth: If one can thoroughly understand this sutra, one should know that all transgressions are eliminated;
seventeenth: If one preaches this sutra, one will be able to attain hundreds of thousands of incalculable Dharma-gates.
Eighteenth: In every lifetime and wherever one may be, one shall not lose the mind of the Way. Nineteenth:

In whatever place one is born, one shall behold the various Buddhas face-to-face and attain the essential *dhāraṇīs* of immeasurable transformations; when such a person contemplates this sutra, Māra Pāpīyas shall never find an opportunity to harm them, and wherever they receive a body, they shall constantly see the Buddhas.

Twentieth: For one who contemplates this sutra, all their aspirations shall surely be fulfilled; bipeds, tripeds, quadrupeds, and venomous insects shall all protect them together. If non-human beings (*amanuṣya*) come with intent to terrify them, or if kings, ministers, *fei-shi* (flying corpses), or evil ghosts come with intent to terrify them, there shall naturally be protection such that none can violate them.
The Buddha said to Mañjuśrī:
“These are the merits of the twenty virtues.

When a bhikṣu who is a Dharma-preacher hears this sutra, he rejoices with firm faith and does not doubt; he harbors no hesitation, but receives, maintains, recites, and cherishes it in his heart. He fully discerns its meaning and explains it for others. Such are his merits.”
Mañjuśrī again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"It is like a medicinal tree named Universal Cure, which is able to eliminate and heal all diseases.
This sutra is likewise; it treats and heals the afflictions of all desires, anger, and ignorance, as well as the maladies of manifold conceptualizations."
The Buddha said to Mañjuśrī:
“What you have said is indeed without error.

This sūtra truly serves to eliminate for all sentient beings the obstructions of the five aggregates, the six sense-decays, the three poisons, the five hindrances, the twelve links of dependent origination, the ninety-six paths, and the sixty-two types of doubt and false views.”
Why is this? In the distant past, in an age long ago, there was a kalpa beyond measure and calculation, exceeding even these numbers.
At that time, there was a Buddha named Rāma-siṃhagati (Joyful Lion’s Gait), who gathered an immeasurable and limitless multitude of people and preached the sūtras within that great assembly.

At that time, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Ratnapadavikrāmin had a bodhisattva named Vajradhvaja. Having heard this sūtra from that Buddha, his mind was free from doubt and hesitation; he immediately accepted and received the merit and power of this sūtra, upholding, reciting, reading, and faithfully studying it, never letting it depart from his mind.
As he traveled through commanderies, kingdoms, counties, towns, villages, provinces, cities, and great states, people saw him and rejoiced, all saying:
"A skilled physician is coming to cure our many ailments."
With single-minded faith and hearts already filled with joy,
at that time a hundred thousand people gathered together and all went to the place where the Bodhisattva Vajradhvaja was, each desiring to seek his protection.

At that time, Vajradhvaja, with a heart of profound faith and compassion, employed the incantations of this sutra for the multitude; taking the various divine mantra phrases from within this scripture, he protected the people with virtue and comforted them, standing as their guardian.
Mañjuśrī! What are those called divine mantra-syllables?
They are recited as follows:

“1. No beating; 2. Separation; 3. Abandoning according to the Vinaya; 4. Skillful deliverance; 5. Non-existence of reality; 6. Absence of location; 7. Freedom from delusion; 8. Honoring the void; 9. Wild as an illusion; 10. Non-arising; 11. Unobtainable; 12. Kind and compassionate; 13. Pitying sentient beings; 14. All that is lowly; 15. Seeking the path; 16. Diligence in the meaning; 17. This is without suffering; 18. This divine mantra. These phrases of the divine mantra shall protect and sustain sentient beings.

Whether one suffers from minor ailments or reaches the point of severe illness, the pain of these manifold afflictions shall be beyond description, yet all such various diseases shall be completely healed and cured.

Those who are harassed by devas, nāgas, spirits, or non-human beings, as well as other venomous insects, pythons, tigers, wolves, mosquitoes, gadflies, and stinging bees—none shall be able to touch them if they maintain compassionate mindfulness of this sutra.
Even those suffering from chronic sores, leprosy, or water-borne diseases shall all be completely healed and cured.
The Buddha said to Mañjuśrī:
"At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Vajradhvaja dwells in this sūtra and heals all the ailments of sentient beings; there are none who do not attain peace and security."
What do you think, Mañjuśrī?
Do you consider the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Vajradhvaja to be anyone other than this person?
Do not hold such a view.
Why is this? It is because I myself am that person.
In that world, I received this sutra, and with firm faith and joyful affection, I upheld, recited, and chanted it, bringing transformation and benefit to all sentient beings.
"Therefore, Mañjuśrī, you should regard this sutra as being like a universal medicinal tree.
Mañjuśrī then asked the Buddha again:
“If there are bodhisattvas who receive the meaning of these divine mantra verses and maintain, recite, and chant them, how should they practice?
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:

“If there are bodhisattvas who receive the meaning of these divine mantra verses and maintain, recite, and chant them, such persons, having resolved their minds to practice this sutra, shall not consume meat, nor shall they anoint or fumigate their bodies with fragrant oils.”
One should always maintain a heart of compassion and pity for all sentient beings, benefiting them all like a universal medicinal tree;
one should always draw near to all-knowledge, the various supernormal powers, and universal wisdom, so that no affliction or harm may find an opportunity to prevail.
If one recites this sutra, one should always keep the mind pure and gentle, free from defiled or turbid conduct.
When chanting this sutra, one should sweep the ground clean so that there is no dust, causing those who see it to feel joy and gladness.
Mañjuśrī again addressed the Buddha, saying:

“If there is a bodhisattva who, when reading this sutra, casts aside craving and does not begrudge his own body or life, treating them as if they were suddenly non-existent, only then does he follow the teaching.”
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī, "It is exactly as you have said; there is not the slightest difference.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Venerable Ānanda:
“Whoever receives this sutra, upholds it, recites it, and reads it, thereby benefiting countless sentient beings—this sutra brings about immeasurable benefit.
Ānanda replied to the Buddha:
“Yes, I understand!”
"You should receive this as the instruction of the Noble Honored One and proclaim it as the teaching of the Buddha.
The Buddha said: "Excellent, excellent!"
“Worthy Ānanda! If one receives this sutra, upholds it, and recites it, they shall perform the work of a Buddha for the sake of all sentient beings.

When the Buddha had spoken thus, the worthy Śāriputra, the worthy Ānanda, Mañjuśrī, the devas, humans, asuras, gandharvas, yakṣas, and nāgas—all who heard what the Buddha said were filled with joy; they paid their respects and departed.
